concepts.name: Origins and Genesis of the Eka Movement (1921–22)
key_dimensions: Geographical epicentre: Hardoi, Bahraich, and Sitapur districts of United Provinces (Awadh region)
Immediate triggers: Excessive rents (50% above recorded rates), illegal levies (nazrana, begar), and share-cropping exploitation
Structural causes: Post-World War I agrarian distress, inflated prices, and failure of Kisan Sabha to address lower peasant grievances
Why it emerged separately from the Non-Cooperation Movement mainstream despite temporal overlap

concepts.name: Leadership of Madari Pasi and Its Significance
key_dimensions: Madari Pasi's background: Low-caste (Pasi community) origin as a distinguishing feature from upper-caste Congress leadership
Contrast with Baba Ramchandra's leadership style and social base in the earlier Awadh Kisan Sabha
Role of local grass-roots mobilisation versus external nationalist leadership
UPSC trap: Madari Pasi vs. Baba Ramchandra — who led which phase/movement in Awadh agrarian unrest

concepts.name: Social Composition and Class Character of the Eka Movement
key_dimensions: Predominantly lower-caste tenants and landless labourers (Pasis, Chamars, Kurmis) — distinct from upper-caste peasant movements
Absence of significant zamindari or taluqdari participation, making it a purely tenant-peasant movement
Role of 'Eka' (unity) oath as a cross-caste mobilisation mechanism
Comparison with Indigo Revolt or Deccan Riots regarding class composition

concepts.name: The 'Eka' Oath Ritual: Content, Symbolism, and Significance
key_dimensions: Sacred ritual nature: Participants swore on water (Ganges water or sacred pond) to pay only recorded rent and resist illegal exactions
Specific pledges: Refusal to pay nazrana (premium), do begar (forced labour), or vacate land on eviction notices
Religious idiom used to mobilise illiterate peasants — significance of using indigenous symbolic frameworks
How the oath created a binding collective commitment that substituted for formal organisation

concepts.name: Demands and Grievances Articulated by the Eka Movement
key_dimensions: Immediate demands: Payment of rent at recorded rates only, abolition of begar, right to pasture lands, end to arbitrary evictions
Distinction between 'legal' rent resistance (recorded rates) and outright non-payment — a moderate but firm position
Absence of demand for land redistribution or zamindari abolition — contrasting with later Telangana or Tebhaga movements
How demands reflected the specific Awadh tenurial structure under the taluqdari system

concepts.name: Relationship Between the Eka Movement and the Non-Cooperation Movement
key_dimensions: Temporal overlap (1921–22) but organisational and ideological distance from Congress-led Non-Cooperation
Congress/Gandhi's ambivalence: Reluctance to associate with radical agrarian mobilisation that threatened propertied classes
Eka movement's autonomy: It did not subordinate itself to Congress discipline or the Gandhian ahimsa framework
UPSC trap: Was Eka Movement part of Non-Cooperation? — Answer: Concurrent but not integrated; Congress kept distance

concepts.name: Role of the Kisan Sabha Network as Precursor and Contrast
key_dimensions: Awadh Kisan Sabha (1920) under Baba Ramchandra as the immediate organisational precursor in the same region
Why Eka emerged: Kisan Sabha's upper-peasant bias left lower castes and bargadars (sharecroppers) underrepresented
Continuity vs. rupture: Eka as a radicalisation and social deepening of the kisan movement in Awadh
Gauri Shankar Mishra and Durgapal Singh's role as Congress-affiliated intermediaries in early Kisan Sabha vs. Eka's independence

concepts.name: The Taluqdari/Zamindari System of Awadh as Structural Context
key_dimensions: Post-1856 annexation settlement: British re-engineered Awadh to create loyal taluqdars, creating exploitative intermediate tenure
Sub-infeudation: Multiple layers between peasant and state, each extracting rent — mahajan, zamindar, taluqdar chain
How the Eka movement targeted the intermediate exploitative layer rather than the colonial state directly
Comparison with Bengal's Permanent Settlement context to distinguish why peasant movements had different characters in both regions

concepts.name: British Colonial Response and Suppression of the Eka Movement
key_dimensions: Deployment of police and military in Hardoi and Bahraich; mass arrests of Eka participants and leaders
Use of the Seditious Meetings Act and criminal intimidation provisions against oath-taking assemblies
Arrest and imprisonment of Madari Pasi as the primary suppression strategy
Contrast with British response to Gandhi-led movements: More brutal, less negotiated — reflecting class/caste bias in colonial administration

concepts.name: Decline and Collapse of the Eka Movement: Causes
key_dimensions: Internal factors: Lack of formal organisation, no permanent leadership structure, dependence on charisma of Madari Pasi
Congress's withdrawal of support and failure to integrate the movement into mainstream nationalist struggle
Suspension of Non-Cooperation after Chauri Chaura (February 1922) demoralised allied peasant activism
Repression-induced fragmentation: Arrest of leaders broke the oath-network without an institutional replacement

concepts.name: Duration and Geographic Spread: The Localised Nature of the Eka Movement
key_dimensions: Confined primarily to three districts: Hardoi, Bahraich, Sitapur — never achieved all-UP or national scale
Why it remained localised: Poor communication infrastructure, caste fragmentation, absence of pan-regional peasant solidarity
Contrast with movements that spread wider (e.g., Mappila Rebellion of 1921 in Malabar) regarding geographic diffusion
Significance of localisation: Shows how agrarian grievances were hyper-local despite shared colonial exploitation

concepts.name: Caste Dimension: Eka as a Lower-Caste Peasant Assertion
key_dimensions: Pasi community's role: A historically marginalised 'criminal tribe' community leading a major agrarian movement
How caste hierarchy within the peasantry prevented upper-caste Kisan Sabhas from representing all tenants
Eka's implicit challenge to both the colonial state AND upper-caste peasant leadership — dual marginality
Historiographical significance: Subaltern studies framework (Ranajit Guha, Gyanendra Pandey) on Eka as subaltern consciousness

concepts.name: Historiography of the Eka Movement: Nationalist vs. Subaltern Perspectives
key_dimensions: Nationalist historiography: Tends to subsume Eka under the broader Non-Cooperation narrative, understating its autonomy
Subaltern Studies (Gyanendra Pandey's work on Awadh peasant movements): Recovers Eka as independent subaltern agency
Marxist interpretation: Eka as an incipient class struggle constrained by religious idiom and lack of revolutionary organisation
UPSC angle: Being able to distinguish what different schools of historiography emphasise about the same movement

concepts.name: Religious and Syncretic Elements in Eka Mobilisation
key_dimensions: Use of Hindu and Muslim religious symbols in oath-taking to forge inter-communal peasant unity
Participation of Muslim peasants and the role of local mullahs alongside Hindu religious figures in Eka meetings
Religious idiom as a double-edged tool: Mobilised effectively but also limited the movement's class-secular articulation
Comparison with Moplah Rebellion (1921) where religious idiom eventually became a barrier to Hindu-Muslim unity

concepts.name: Eka Movement vs. Mappila (Moplah) Rebellion: Comparative Analysis
key_dimensions: Both in 1921 — temporal simultaneity but vastly different character, leadership, and outcome
Eka: Multi-caste Hindu-Muslim peasant unity; Mappila: Predominantly Muslim peasant movement with religious overtones
Congress response: Supported Mappila initially (Khilafat link) but distanced from both when violence erupted
UPSC trap: Distinguishing the two contemporary agrarian movements in terms of causes, leadership, and historical assessment

concepts.name: Eka Movement vs. Awadh Kisan Sabha vs. Oudh Rent (Amendment) Act 1921: Policy Context
key_dimensions: Oudh Rent (Amendment) Act 1921: Colonial concession that gave some occupancy rights but was inadequate for bargadars
Whether the Act was a response to or independent of the peasant agitations in Awadh
Limitations of the Act that kept grievances alive and provided fuel for the Eka movement
Pattern of colonial legislative response to agrarian unrest — compare with Bengal Tenancy Act (1885) pattern

concepts.name: Legacy and Long-term Impact of the Eka Movement
key_dimensions: Contribution to peasant political consciousness in UP: Laid groundwork for later Congress Agrarian Programme and Nehru's engagement with peasant issues
Influenced the formation of All India Kisan Sabha (1936) by demonstrating the need for organised peasant representation
Exposed the class contradiction within Indian nationalism — forced Congress to eventually articulate agrarian reform demands
Why it is considered a 'failed' movement yet historically significant: Short-term defeat, long-term contribution to agrarian discourse

concepts.name: Begar (Forced Labour) as a Central Grievance: Context and Resistance
key_dimensions: Definition and forms of begar in Awadh: Free labour service to zamindars/taluqdars for construction, harvest, domestic work
Legal ambiguity: Begar was not explicitly legalised but informally enforced through social coercion and economic dependency
Eka's pledge to refuse begar as a direct challenge to the labour-exploitation dimension of the agrarian system
Comparison: Begar resistance in Kumaon (1921, Gandhian-led) vs. Eka movement's begar resistance — different methods, same grievance

concepts.name: Role of Women in the Eka Movement
key_dimensions: Participation of lower-caste women in Eka oath meetings — departure from upper-caste purdah norms
Women as enforcers of the Eka oath within households and villages: Social pressure mechanism
Absence of women in formal leadership: Glass ceiling even within subaltern movements
Comparison with women's participation in Tebhaga (1946–47) and Telangana movements to assess evolution of gender roles in peasant struggles

concepts.name: Nazrana (Premium/Forced Gift) System as Trigger: Economic Mechanism of Exploitation
key_dimensions: Definition: Illegal premium demanded by zamindars over and above recorded rent at time of lease renewal or transfer
Economic impact: Could equal 6–12 months of rent, pushing tenants into debt bondage to mahajans
Legal status: Nazrana was NOT recognised under tenancy law but was extracted through extra-legal coercion
Why Eka specifically targeted nazrana: It was the most visible symbol of arbitrary power that exceeded even colonial law — making resistance legally defensible
